big: Meena buys 500 shares at ₹100.40 and, a minute later, changes her mind and sells at ₹100.00. The price did not move at all, yet she lost ₹200. The gap between the two prices has a name.

lines: Nothing changed, yet I lost money. How?
Every share has two prices at any moment: what buyers offer and what sellers ask. The gap between them is a cost of trading. Liquid shares have a small gap. Thinly traded ones have a wide gap.

note: This is before brokerage and taxes, which come on top.

title: Settlement and prices
stops: India settles most trades one working day after the trade
The bid is what a seller asks
A price band limits how far a share can move in a day
Market capitalisation is the share price alone
caps: T+1 means shares and money change hands on the next working day.
The bid is the highest price a buyer offers. The ask is the seller's price.
When a share hits its band, trading in it is halted or restricted for the day.
Market capitalisation is price multiplied by the number of shares.

q: Rohan buys shares on Monday. When do they usually reach his demat account under T+1?
why: Under T+1, shares and money change hands on the next working day.
The shares take a working day to settle, not a minute.
A month is far longer than the standard settlement for shares.
A year is nowhere near the usual settlement time.

q: A share shows a bid of ₹100.00 and an ask of ₹100.40. Meena buys and sells at once. What happens?
opts: She gains the gap on each share
She pays no cost at all
She loses the gap on each share
The exchange adds the gap to her demat
why: The gap works against the person who buys and sells straight away.
The gap is a real cost, though brokerage and tax come on top.
She buys at the ask and sells at the bid, so the gap is a loss on each share.
The exchange does not add the gap to her holdings.

q: A stock hits its daily upper price band. What may follow?
opts: Its price doubles in the next hour
Trading in it is restricted that day
why: A band stops moves beyond a set limit, so doubling is not likely.
SEBI does not refund buyers when a stock reaches its band.
Reaching a band does not shut a company down in any way.
A band limits the move, and hitting it restricts trading.

q: A company has 200 crore shares at ₹50 each. What is its market capitalisation?
why: ₹250 crore adds the two numbers together, which is not how it works.
Market cap is price times shares, so 200 crore times ₹50 is ₹10,000 crore.
₹50 crore is just the price, and it ignores the number of shares.
₹200 crore is just the number of shares and ignores the price.

pts: T+1: shares and money change hands the next working day.
The bid-ask gap is a hidden cost of trading.
A price band limits the daily move. Market cap is price times shares.
